claims.claim: Harrison describes Kay's affect as magic but little mystery, a platonic ideal of Tang China described with precision and thoroughness.
Harrison says Tai's absurdly ambitious mourning is credible only when rendered within Kay's stately narrative.
Harrison notes that in the final third the implied narrator becomes a real narrator and the focus pulls back, making the novel a threnody and one telling among many.

claims.claim: Harrison notes the horse-gift frame keeps expected big set-piece events off-stage in favour of the feel of a moment of historical possibility.

verdicts.trueWording: Dunnett did this “by having him... say things the reader doesn’t understand”
verdicts.note: Locus page reached raw (curl, HTTP 200). Quote is verbatim: “one of the ways she did it is by having him, or sometimes other people, say things the reader doesn’t understand.” But Kay presents this strictly as Dorothy Dunnett’s technique in the Lymond books, admired in the context of how hard it is “to convey the idea that a character is genuinely smart.” Nowhere on the page does he say he borrows or uses the device himself.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Kay borrows/adopts the method for his own fiction — the page attributes it to Dunnett only

verdicts.trueWording: “One of them will be the supernatural. Another might be the erotic… lyric language.”
verdicts.note: Locus raw page. Quote “another might be lyric language” appears verbatim (“…and another might be lyric language”). Full list is on the page — supernatural, erotic, intrigue, suspense, lyric language — framed as “various elements that an author has available to work with” answering “what does this story demand, require… What does this book need from me”. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “I did a bad troubadour early in A Song for Arbonne”
verdicts.note: Locus raw page. “It’s fun writing a bad writer, too” is verbatim, immediately followed by “I did a bad troubadour early in A Song for Arbonne, and it’s ridiculously enjoyable to hack around with a hack’s work.” Both limbs (enjoyment; the Arbonne troubadour) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “the unwritten lives of women, and of the poor”
verdicts.note: Locus raw page: “I’ve talked often about looking for the unwritten histories, the people at the margins of history, and this has been part of my fiction forever. The unwritten lives of women, and of the poor.” Quote verbatim; every limb supported. (Page adds he also loves “the chronicles of the dukes and the popes” — not exclusive ways of looking.)

verdicts.trueWording: “I think every serious writer is teaching a reader how to read them.”
verdicts.note: Locus raw page. Sentence appears in full, verbatim, opening its paragraph. Claim is an exact restatement.

verdicts.trueWording: “I’m always wary, though, of proposing clear ‘lessons’.”
verdicts.note: Live reactormag.com returned HTTP 403 to both a plain and a full browser-header request; recovered raw via Wayback id_ capture 20221207110311 of the original tor.com URL. Quote “times and places on the cusp of transition” verbatim; borderlands limb verbatim (“Borderlands have always been, for me, compelling in that way”); wariness limb verbatim. Words are Kay’s, quoted from the io9 interview.

verdicts.trueWording: “my ‘emperor’ is inspired by Rudolph II… about a century after ‘my’ core period”
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture. Quote “let me make use of some elements I couldn’t have” verbatim (“One thing the quarter turn does… is let me make use of some elements I couldn’t have in a straight history”). Children/Rudolph II and the century-out-of-period limbs both verbatim on the page. Note the page says “inspired by” where the claim says “modelled on” — same force.

verdicts.trueWording: “Period and place, and theme, then characters. The narrative arc emerges from these.”
verdicts.note: Psychopomp raw page (HTTP 200), interview dated December 9, 2008, matching the c. 2008 attribution. “I don’t outline the books.” verbatim. Ordering limb supported, with the page reading “Period and place, and theme, then characters” (‘and theme’ rather than the claim’s ‘then theme’) — same list, same sequence.

verdicts.trueWording: “Dorothy was unmatched at the revelation of character through action”
verdicts.note: Psychopomp raw page: “Dorothy was unmatched at the revelation of character through action, as opposed to stopping a narrative to ‘do’ the character-stuff, which so many writers (and that includes the serious ones) end up doing.” Quote verbatim; ‘unmatched’ and ‘rather than stopping the narrative’ limbs both explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: “the extravagance of his vision might be better expressed as one of the poems”
verdicts.note: Vector raw page (HTTP 200), dated August 18, 2010. Quote “Kay’s superlative-rich style risks beauty fatigue” verbatim; the poems limb follows in the same sentence. Byline on the page reads only “Niall” (Niall Harrison, Vector’s reviewer/editor) — the surname is not printed on the page, but the review content is fully as attributed.

verdicts.trueWording: “a platonic ideal of Tang China… all described with precision and thoroughness”
verdicts.note: Vector raw page. “This affect — magic but little mystery — is familiar from the other Kay novel I’ve read” is verbatim; the preceding paragraph has “Kay’s creation can be what you might call a platonic ideal of Tang China: a world of heart-stopping beauty… all described with precision and thoroughness.” Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “whose duration and ambition would be absurd if not rendered within Kay’s stately narrative”
verdicts.note: Vector raw page. Quote “rendered within Kay’s stately narrative” verbatim; the page’s ‘would be absurd if not rendered within’ is exactly the claim’s ‘credible only when rendered within’. Subject is Shen Tai’s ritual mourning, as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: “this telling is only one among an endless series of interpretations”
verdicts.note: Vector raw page. Quote verbatim. All five elements are on the page in one passage: ‘Under Heaven’s final third’, ‘the implied narrator becomes a real narrator’, ‘the focus gradually pulls back’, ‘the novel is a threnody for a culture… choosing to diminish’, ‘only one among an endless series’. The page phrases the threnody as ‘confirmed’ in the final third alongside the narrator shift rather than caused by it; the claim’s ‘making’ is a compression, not an added fact.

verdicts.trueWording: “keeps some of what might be expected to be big set-piece events off-stage”
verdicts.note: Vector raw page. Quote “big set-piece events off-stage” verbatim, of the horse-gift frame (‘it’s the existence of the horses that shapes the story… It’s an interesting frame’). Historical-possibility limb verbatim: ‘less interested in capturing those than he is in describing the feel of a moment of historical possibility’. The page qualifies with ‘some of’, which the claim drops — a softening, not a contradiction.

verdicts.trueWording: “not something specific to his depiction of Kitai”
verdicts.note: Vector raw page, comment by ‘Niall’ dated August 19, 2010 at 7:34 am, replying to Kate Nepveu. Quote “the elevated register is characteristic of Kay’s work” verbatim, continuing “not something specific to his depiction of Kitai”. Both limbs and the ‘in comments’ framing supported; note he prefixes it ‘as you say’, endorsing the commenter’s point in his own words.
